items.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. items.title: [AINews] Building AIE CODE: The top Coding Agent Conference
items.content: It’s a quiet day, so as we have done once per conference, we’ll do a behind the scenes look at AI Engineer , now serving 6M views a month for 1.8M monthly unique viewers . CODE is the last flagship AIE of the year (there are also 2 partner conferences coming up - AIEi Shanghai takes place next week, and AIEi Sydney is a side event of NeurIPS in December). As a Summit it is meant to be more intimate: single track, invite-only for the top 1000 agentic engineers in the world (over 100k tuned into our Software Factories track at WF26 ). My goal in curating AIE CODE is to try to recap the top themes of 2026 in code and gather the leaders of the industry to preview what’s next in 2027. Last year we had some absolute bangers building Skills and Software Factories , predicting the death of the IDE and of course the launch of Antigravity and Nano Banana Pro. We have three themes this year: Scaling without Slop : Last year’s call for No More Slop has resulted in lots of discussions about managing it this year, including the rise and fall of Tokenmaxxing . Our Scaling without Slop approach has mostly worked; we need more. System One models : We believe S1 “smart software” is the largest change to AI Engineering that refreshingly explores the opposite direction to ever larger and more expensive and questionably productive swarms of coding agent FactoryFactoryFactories. While Diogo took pains to explain the difference between Decision Models and System One models on our podcast and his WF26 talk , it has largely been lost to the broader audience. Diogo and team TypeSafe are back for a mini “Jev Day” to show how System One models are truly being used by their top users. Increasing Ambition: This year we also saw increasingly ambitious rewrites of some of the hardest categories of software, from browsers to Adobe PhotoShop Suite to mid-tier B2B SaaS . items.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
items.content: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian,   provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape.  DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital.   Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.3…
items.summary: A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images.

items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.content: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the applica…
items.summary: Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson on building the backend for AI agents

items.title: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?
items.content: Zilan Qian is a research scholar at GovAI researching AI development and regulation in China. On October 21, the People’s Daily published a commentary titled “Turning ‘Gunpowder’ into ‘Fireworks’? Beware the Claim That China’s AI Has Gone Astray” (把”火药”做成”烟花”？警惕”中国AI跑偏论”). The same day, Nanfang Commentary (南方评论), the op-ed column of Southern Daily , asked : “Is Half of China’s Compute Being Spent on Feel-Good Dramas (爽剧)? Don’t Judge AI by Its Tokens.” Three days earlier, Beijing News (新京报) had questioned whether “‘American AI Boosts Productivity While Chinese AI Makes Tittytainment’ Is a False Proposition.” All three state-affiliated outlets were responding to the same viral claim: that 55% of China’s AI tokens were being used for short dramas and video generation. The claim struck a nerve because AI-generated entertainment in China is both everywhere and widely despised. According to China’s broadcasting regulator, more than 90% of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. Yet Chinese media and public figures routinely call them wunao (无脑, braindead), cuzhi lanzao (粗制滥造, shoddily made), and zhili dixia (智力低下, intellectually deficient). 1 Why, in a society that places such a premium on productivity, has an industry devoted to manufacturing seemingly useless pleasure become so enormously popular? And what should we make of the shame attached to it? I argue that both answers lie in Chinese society’s obsession with usefulness, where technologies and people alike are judged by their productive value, so much so that resting can feel…
items.summary: The 55% token myth, and China’s guilty pleasure

items.title: Xi vs Trump on Corruption
items.content: In February, Eric and Donald Jr. sat down with a reporter to explain why Abu Dhabi paid $500m for a stake in World Liberty Financial. Don Jr. said, “They tried all this nonsense the first time around. Frankly, it’s gotten old…They created this monster.” The monster of political corruption has been with us since the founding. But since the Progressive Eva, it has been cut with at least a tinge of embarrassment. The Trumps instead have done it in broad daylight and tried to make it a flex. China’s political system is riddled with corruption on an entirely different scale. The skims in China happen up and down the system, and making a billion dollars while in office is nothing new for senior Chinese leaders. But Xi understands what this costs the Party. In his first Politburo speech as General Secretary, he warned that corruption, left to spread, would “doom the Party and the state.” Xi was horrified by seeing youth with bloodlines just as red as his crash foreign sports cars in the streets of Beijing. He views the princeling inheritance as a responsibility to serve, not a license to fuckboy. As Kamil Galeev writes , Xi aims to extirpate “the alien, unfamiliar, threatening bandit entrepreneurial culture — not even from the country but rather, from the national elites.” Xi is a believer, but Trump is a businessman. After Trump brought down the guardrails with a compliant SCOTUS and Congress, the presidential family has been sloppily revenue-maximizing ever since. 1 Xi’s anti-corruption campaign hasn’t liquidated corruption in China, which still lubricates a much higher percentage of economic activity than similar behavior does in America. But Xi has succeeded in making it dangerous. Making outside money in Xi’s China runs the risk of execution — far different stakes than embarrassing ProPublica articles revealing crimes that get pardoned away. Make corruption cringe again! At least Chin…
items.summary: The Shame Gap

items.title: The Manhattan Project, Take Two
items.content: In the new era of global competition, being at the forefront of Super Intelligence innovation equals geopolitical power. To maintain leadership and establish the next world order, the U.S. is moving to cement its lead. Barnett Koven is a Managing Director of AI and Data at Accenture Federal Services . He came to Accenture Federal Services after stints in industry and a faculty job at the University of Maryland, where his counterinsurgency research showed that some of the most influential quantitative studies got the answer exactly backwards. We discuss… Why “inaction is in and of itself risky” — and how government risk-aversion compounds against less-cautious competitors The “gun-armor race” in classified AI environments, where defense costs grow exponentially against linear offense Entity resolution and predictive modeling for BIS export-control enforcement, and unwrapping the PLA’s shell-company maze DOE’s Genesis Mission and Accenture Federal’s “backbone for scientific research” Thank you to Accenture Federal Services for bringing us this episode. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . From COIN to Genesis Jordan Schneider: Let’s do a bit of the career arc. How do we get from a PhD on COIN to DOE and the Genesis mission? Barnett Koven: Absolutely. I spent a lot of time in Latin America and saw the aftereffects of some virulent insurgencies in Peru and Colombia in particular, ended up doing a PhD studying the spatiotemporal diffusion of insurgent violence as a result of counterinsurgency strategy — specifically as a result of development assistance and other non-kinetic interventions during counterinsurgency. Really loved that, and sought out the opportunity to do more policy-relevant research, which is not necessarily the norm at the academy. Ended up in a faculty job at the University of Maryland, which was also wonderful — a research institution where I was encouraged and ab…
items.summary: Barnett Koven on American innovation and Super Intelligence

items.title: Roasting China’s AI Industry
items.content: Xianyu (咸鱼), the writer behind 葬AI — “Funeral AI” — produces some of my favorite satire about China’s AI industry. ChinaTalk readers may remember his essay “Open Models Are the United Front of AI” . In this conversation, we talk about: Why AI writing isn’t funny; How Xianyu made a website for ordinary people to rank video model by meme-ability; Why Five Year Plans are a kind of benchmark; And why there’s so much Chinglish in AI. We also disagree about where the hype is worse: China or America. The conversation is in Mandarin. Listen to the original audio here, or read a lightly abridged English translation of the transcript below. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. On Writing Humor Irene: Xianyu, welcome to ChinaTalk. I’ve been a devoted fan since your essay on Juche AI last September, so it’s a real honor to have you here. Could you introduce yourself? When did you start writing, and how did you get into independent publishing? Xianyu: Before we begin, I just need to get it on record: Juche is a glorious ideology. I started writing Funeral AI last July or August, approaching AI through subculture. A lot of people in the AI industry maybe didn’t quite understand that. If you have a purely technical background, you may prefer very serious, professional articles. But from the beginning, I thought that even the most advanced technology — the models and APIs that frontier labs spend tens of billions of dollars developing — is available at a relatively affordable consumer price, perhaps $20 or $100. So any ordinary person has the right to describe how it feels to use AI. That was my starting point. And it has proved true: even with the most advanced AI, including GPT-6, which came out a few days ago, or the hottest venture-backed projects, an ordinary person without a te…
